title: Drive-by Compromise — Behavior-based, Multi-platform Detection Strategy (T1189)
summary: This strategy detects drive-by compromise, where an adversary compromises a website or its advertising content so that merely visiting the page causes a browser or browser plugin to run attacker code. The technique is hard to catch at the moment of delivery because the malicious content is served by a site the user trusts, so detection leans on the client side chain: browser or office application spawning an unexpected child process, script interpreters launched by a browser, new executables written to user download or temporary directories followed by execution, and proxy or secure web gateway records of a redirect chain that ends at an exploit kit pattern. The common failure is that modern browsers generate many legitimate child processes and script hosts, so precision depends on correlating the parent chain, the file path and the outbound connection destination rather than any single event.

beginner.definition: A drive-by compromise means a person visits a normal looking website and gets infected without clicking anything. The website or its adverts were tampered with. This detection looks for the strange behaviours that follow in the browser on the user's computer.
beginner.whyItMatters: The user did nothing wrong, so training and warnings do not help. Trusted sites are used, so web blocking lists are not enough. It can affect many staff in a short time if the site is popular at your company. Catching the browser behaviour fast limits how many computers are harmed.
howItWorks: The browser writes records of pages it visits, and the network records the addresses it connects to.
The operating system writes an event when any program starts, including which program started it.
The detection looks for a browser or an office program starting a script host, such as a PowerShell or Windows Script Host process.
It also looks for a new executable written into a download or temporary folder and started soon after.
The network records are checked for a chain of redirects that ends at a host with a poor reputation, or that serves a file instead of a page.
When the process chain and the network chain agree on the same time and the same computer, the alert is raised for review.
beginner.example: Think of a food market where one stall's sign is swapped overnight. Shoppers follow the sign in good faith and buy from the wrong stall. The shoppers did nothing careless. Only comparing the sign with the market's official map shows the swap.
takeaways: Drive-by compromise needs no user mistake, so you cannot train it away.
Look at what the browser started, not only at which site it visited.
Correlate the redirect chain with the process chain on the same host and time.

objectives: Explain how a trusted website or advert can deliver exploitation without user interaction
Identify browser and office parent child process patterns that indicate script execution
Correlate proxy redirect chains with local file creation and process execution on the same host
Use reputation and content type signals to separate exploit delivery from normal browsing
Prioritise containment actions that stop further infection from the same delivery host
dataSources: Sysmon event 1 process creation recording browser and office application parent images with full command lines
Sysmon event 11 file creation for executables written to download, temporary and user profile directories
Secure web gateway or proxy logs recording request chains, response content types and destination reputation
Sysmon event 3 network connection records linking browser child processes to external destinations
Browser download history and extension inventory collected by endpoint management agents
logic: The detection links a browsing session to code execution on the same host within a short window. The fields that must be correlated are the browser or office parent image, the child process it spawned, the file path created just before that child started, the destination address of the outbound connection, and the response content type recorded by the proxy. A benign case shows a browser opening a helper process for a known plugin or an office application opening a document with no subsequent script host and no executable written to a download directory. The malicious case shows a script interpreter or script host spawned directly by the browser, a newly created executable in a download or temporary path, and a redirect chain that ends at a host serving an executable or a page from a recently registered or low reputation domain.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Browser Or Office Process Spawns Script Host After File Download
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: sysmon
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 1
#     ParentImage|endswith:
#       - \chrome.exe
#       - \msedge.exe
#       - \winword.exe
#       - \excel.exe
#     Image|endswith:
#       - \powershell.exe
#       - \wscript.exe
#       - \cscript.exe
#       - \mshta.exe
#       - \rundll32.exe
#   filter:
#     CommandLine|contains:
#       - '\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\'
#       - 'update check'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: Single sign-on and multifactor authentication browser extensions that launch a local helper process to complete login
Corporate intranet pages that intentionally open a scripted launcher for an approved internal application
Password managers and video conferencing plugins that start a local service from the browser
Software update pages that download and run a signed installer with the browser as the parent process
Web based administrative consoles that use a script host to apply local configuration on managed workstations
tuningNotes: Start by recording every child process that browsers and office applications legitimately create in your environment, then allow list those specific image and command line combinations with their signer, and alert on everything else. Add the proxy response content type as a joining field so that downloads of signed internal installers can be suppressed while unsigned content from low reputation hosts cannot. Scoping the rule to endpoints in sensitive groups, such as finance and administrators, reduces triage volume but leaves the wider fleet exposed, so keep a fleet wide version that only alerts when the script host also makes an outbound connection to a destination outside your normal browsing profile.
